Triggers.value: Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try to erase the memory of the event
constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I have failed in my most important role in life
My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: 'Being in nature similar to where it happened' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of life-threatening illness, which typically involves medical/health contexts rather than a natural-environment trauma setting.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies bereavement/loss of another person, which does not fit the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness unless there is an unreported death-related trauma; it is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: 'Fear of rage' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile: the other appraisals and memory items center on damage, unreality, and role failure after illness, not anger-based dyscontrol. This makes the appraisal set less internally coherent.

vignette: Aisha Patel, a 42‑year‑old project manager in a New York advertising firm, has been living with the aftershocks of a sudden, life‑threatening illness that left her in an intensive‑care unit for almost a month. On a rainy spring morning, her phone buzzed with a frantic call from a friend: “Your mom is choking—call an ambulance.” Aisha dashed out, only to be rushed to the ER where the air smelled of antiseptic and the fluorescent lights hummed like a distant drum. She was intubated, tubes were threaded into her neck, and the cold, metal‑faced environment seemed to seep into her bones. The memory of the ICU, with its stark white walls and the clack of needles on the drip set, is still vivid for Aisha, yet she feels it too extreme to believe, as if the event had occurred in someone else’s story. The very scent of disinfectant and the chill of the hospital air now act as triggers that pull her back into that moment. When she first encountered a whiff of cleaning solution in her office or felt a sudden drop in temperature during a meeting, the image of the cold ICU burst forth, and with it a wave of dread. Those triggers immediately pushed her toward the maladaptive strategies she has come to rely on. Aisha began to keep her eyes fixed on the ceiling, mentally erasing the memory of the event whenever it intruded. She also started to hyper‑monitor her own thoughts, convinced that a slip into panic could mean the return of her life‑threatening illness. In addition, she has gone so far as to avoid any hospital or ambulance, even when her husband’s mother needed a routine physical. The triggers, by virtue of their sensory specificity, also sharpen Aisha’s memory of the trauma. The smell of antiseptic in a cleaning product or the cold feel of a draft during a cold front on the street reawaken the fragmented recollection of the ICU. Yet because she believes that her life was destroyed and that she has failed in her most vital role as a provider and project lead, that memory feels even more crushing. Her sense of physical vulnerability—her body still “damaged” by the illness—further magnifies the emotional weight of the recollected moments. As the memory blazes in her mind, it reinforces her negative appraisal that her life is ruined, that she has failed, and that she is permanently exposed to danger. Simultaneously, each time she recollects the ICU, the very smell, the cold air, and the sight of needles surface again as triggers, creating a tight feedback loop that keeps her stuck in a state of hyper‑awareness. Aisha’s attempts to erase the memory and constantly check her thoughts have, paradoxically, maintained the memory’s presence. The act of trying to forget keeps the story alive in a fragmented form—some details are crystal clear while others remain blank, which in turn makes the memory feel unreal and impossible to dismiss. Her avoidance of medical cues has only intensified her sensitivity to them; a quick sniff of cleaning fluid or the sight of a stethoscope now feels like a prelude to disaster, pushing her further into a state of hyper‑monitoring. This avoidance also underpins her belief that she has failed, as she sees herself as unable to face the very symbols of medical care she once trusted. The cycle has taken a toll on her professional life. Aisha now frequently reschedules meetings to avoid the office’s air‑conditioning drafts, and she has started to miss deadlines because she can’t focus when she feels a trigger in the air. Her husband, seeing her withdrawal, has become frustrated, which adds to her fear that she is not fulfilling her role as a partner. These strains have deepened her belief that her life has been ruined, and she feels trapped by the impossible task of navigating both a demanding job and a life under constant threat. Aisha finally reached out for help after a particularly painful episode in which a faint scent of cleaning solution at her coworker’s desk triggered a panic attack that left her gasping for breath, unable to complete a presentation. She woke that night with the feeling that she might lose her job, her marriage, or even her life again. She hopes therapy can help her untangle the web of triggers, maladaptive strategies, memory, and negative appraisals that have kept her in a state of constant threat, and she fears that without intervention she will continue to sabotage her own health and career.
